title: Prompting Techniques & Control
description: Core prompt engineering principles, few-shot prompting as in-context demonstration, controlling style and format explicitly, and using iterative refinement instead of one-shot perfection.

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering: Treating the Prompt as an Interface
lessons.description: Learn the core principles of writing prompts that reliably get what you want.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can list a few concrete techniques for making a prompt more likely to produce the output you want.

sections.title: 📝 The prompt is the only interface you have
sections.content: Unlike a traditional function with typed parameters, a generative model's only input is (mostly) natural language. This means the prompt itself has to carry everything the model needs: what task to do, what format to respond in, what tone to use, and what context is relevant.

sections.title: 🧱 Concrete techniques that consistently help
sections.content:
Be **specific** about format and constraints rather than vague ('respond with exactly 3 bullet points' beats 'give me some thoughts'). Provide **context** the model needs but doesn't already have (relevant background, definitions of unusual terms). Separate **instructions from content** clearly (so the model doesn't confuse your instructions for content to process, or vice versa).

```python
# Vague:
prompt = "Tell me about this"

# Specific:
prompt = (
    "Summarize the following support ticket in exactly 2 sentences, "
    "focused on the customer's core complaint:\n\n{ticket_text}"
)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming a prompt that worked once will always work identically.** Sampling randomness (temperature, top-p from earlier in this course) means the same prompt can produce somewhat different outputs across runs.

**Writing a vague prompt and blaming the model for a vague result.** Much of what looks like a model limitation is actually an underspecified prompt.

**Overloading a single prompt with too many unrelated instructions at once.** Breaking a complex task into smaller, more focused prompts (or steps) is often more reliable than one giant instruction.

codeSnippet.code:
# Vague:
prompt = "Tell me about this"

# Specific:
prompt = (
    "Summarize the following support ticket in exactly 2 sentences, "
    "focused on the customer's core complaint:\n\n{ticket_text}"
)

lessons.title: Few-Shot Prompting: Showing Instead of Telling
lessons.description: Use examples inside the prompt itself to demonstrate the exact pattern you want.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what few-shot prompting is and when it tends to outperform a plain instruction.

sections.title: 👀 Show, don't just tell
sections.content:
**Zero-shot** prompting gives only an instruction, with no examples. **Few-shot** prompting includes a handful of example input-output pairs directly in the prompt, demonstrating the exact pattern desired — format, tone, level of detail — often more effectively than describing that pattern in words alone.

```python
prompt = '''
Classify the sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral.

Text: "I loved this movie!"
Sentiment: positive

Text: "It was okay, nothing special."
Sentiment: neutral

Text: "Worst purchase I've ever made."
Sentiment:
'''
```

sections.title: 🎯 Why examples work so well
sections.content: This connects directly to the in-context learning idea covered in the LLM engineering track: a model conditions its next-token predictions on everything in its context, including the example pairs — so a well-chosen set of examples effectively steers the output pattern without any weight updates or fine-tuning at all.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Using inconsistent or contradictory examples.** If your few-shot examples don't follow a consistent pattern themselves, the model has nothing reliable to imitate.

**Using too many examples and running into context length limits.** Each example costs tokens (recall the LLM engineering track's discussion of context windows and cost) — there's a real tradeoff between more examples and prompt size.

**Choosing examples that don't represent the range of real inputs.** If all your examples are easy cases, the model has no guidance for handling harder or edge-case inputs it will actually encounter.

codeSnippet.code:
prompt = '''
Classify the sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral.

Text: "I loved this movie!"
Sentiment: positive

Text: "It was okay, nothing special."
Sentiment: neutral

Text: "Worst purchase I've ever made."
Sentiment:
'''

lessons.title: Controlling Style, Tone, and Output Format
lessons.description: Explicitly steer a model's voice and structure instead of hoping it guesses correctly.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can name a few concrete ways to control a generative model's tone and output format.

sections.title: 🎭 Role and persona framing
sections.content: Framing part of the prompt as a role or persona ('You are a concise technical writer...') sets expectations for tone and style that carry through the whole response, functioning similarly to a system prompt in the LLM engineering track's terminology — policy set once, applied throughout the generation.

sections.title: 📐 Explicit format constraints work better than implicit hints
sections.content:
Rather than hoping the model infers a desired structure, state it directly: word/sentence counts, required sections, output as a numbered list vs. prose, or (connecting to the earlier lesson on constrained decoding) an actual schema for machine-readable output.

```python
prompt = (
    "Write a product description in exactly 3 short paragraphs: "
    "one on features, one on use cases, one on who it's for. "
    "Use a friendly, non-technical tone."
)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming style instructions are 'sticky' forever in a long conversation.** In longer multi-turn interactions, tone can drift; restating key style constraints periodically can help.

**Conflating format control with content control.** Telling a model *how* to format an answer doesn't guarantee the *content* itself is correct — those are separate concerns.

**Using soft style hints when a hard constraint is actually needed.** For anything that must be machine-parseable, prefer the constrained decoding approach from earlier over a style suggestion alone.

codeSnippet.code:
prompt = (
    "Write a product description in exactly 3 short paragraphs: "
    "one on features, one on use cases, one on who it's for. "
    "Use a friendly, non-technical tone."
)

**Conflating format control with content control.** Telling a model *how* to format an answer doesn't guarantee the *content* itself is correct — those are separate concerns.

**Using soft style hints when a hard constraint is actually needed.** For anything that must be machine-parseable, prefer the constrained decoding approach from earlier over a style suggestion alone.

lessons.title: Iterative Refinement: Treating Generation as a Conversation
lessons.description: Use follow-up prompts to refine an output instead of trying to get it perfect in one shot.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why iterative refinement is often more effective than trying to write the perfect single prompt.

sections.title: 🔁 One prompt rarely nails it on the first try
sections.content: Rather than treating generation as a single, one-shot request that must be perfect, iterative refinement treats it as a short conversation: get an initial output, then give targeted feedback ('make the second paragraph shorter', 'use a more formal tone') to steer it closer to what you actually want.

sections.title: 🎯 Targeted feedback beats starting over
sections.content:
Specific, targeted feedback on what to change is usually far more effective than regenerating from scratch with a slightly reworded original prompt — the model has the previous output as context and can make a precise, localized edit rather than guessing at the whole thing again.

```python
# Less effective: rewrite the whole prompt and hope for a better result
# More effective: "Keep everything the same, but shorten paragraph 2 to one sentence."
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Trying to perfect a single mega-prompt instead of iterating.** For complex outputs, iteration is often faster and more reliable than one exhaustively detailed initial prompt.

**Giving vague refinement feedback ('make it better').** Refinement feedback benefits from the same specificity principle as an initial prompt — say exactly what should change.

**Forgetting context length limits during long refinement conversations.** A long back-and-forth eventually accumulates enough tokens to hit the context window limits covered in the LLM engineering track.
